slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 27: Appendix F — Working Vocabulary and Design Questions. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

question.prompt: What is the central teaching rule for Modern C++?
question.answer: Do not praise an abstraction until you can explain the rule it encodes and the evidence that proves it behaves correctly.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Appendix F — Working Vocabulary and Design Questions changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

question.prompt: Why is “it compiled” not enough evidence?
question.answer: Compilation proves the source met translation rules, but it does not prove the intended runtime behavior, output contract, state invariant, or test case.

slides.narration: Read this roadmap as a dependency chain. The chapter begins with the conceptual reason for the feature, then moves into the concrete rule, then tests the rule through examples. As the teacher, keep asking which boundary is being protected: ownership, lifetime, mutability, type validity, algorithm range, or release evidence. The path through the chapter should make the final example feel inevitable rather than decorative.

slides.title: F.1 Values, owners, and borrows
keyPoints: Value semantics.
An object behaves as a meaningful value under its documented copying, comparison, and mutation rules.
Independent value copies are a design goal for many domain types, but shared or borrowed members can change those.
Ask whether modifying one copy can affect another through an alias.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 27, treat F.1 Values, owners, and borrows as a design decision with costs and evidence. Value semantics. An object behaves as a meaningful value under its documented copying, comparison, and mutation rules. Independent value copies are a design goal for many domain types, but shared or borrowed members can change those semantics. Ask whether modifying one copy can affect another through an alias. Owner. The object or subsystem responsible for a resource’s lifetime. Ownership includes responsibility for release, not merely permission to access. Ask which exact destructor or explicit completion path ends that responsibility and whether another object can accidentally release the same resource. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: F.2 Interfaces and guarantees
keyPoints: Class invariant.
A relationship that valid observable states of a class must satisfy.
Ask which operations can change the relevant members and where validation occurs before those changes become.
A comment saying “valid range” is weaker than an interface that prevents invalid mutation.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 27, treat F.2 Interfaces and guarantees as a design decision with costs and evidence. Class invariant. A relationship that valid observable states of a class must satisfy. Ask which operations can change the relevant members and where validation occurs before those changes become public. A comment saying “valid range” is weaker than an interface that prevents invalid mutation. Strong exception guarantee. Failure preserves the specified observable state. Ask where that state boundary ends: input positions, diagnostics, counters, and remote effects can lie outside it. A guarantee without a named boundary is easy to overstate. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 27, treat F.3 Traversal, algorithms, and result models as a design decision with costs and evidence. Iterator invalidation. A change that makes a previously obtained iterator unusable under the relevant container or range rules. Ask about cached end iterators as well as element iterators, and distinguish iterator stability from the stability of an element’s logical identity. Projection. A function selecting the part of an element used by a range algorithm. Ask whether the projected value owns its data or borrows it and whether comparison over the projected domain satisfies the algorithm’s requirements. Strict weak ordering. The semantic ordering relationship required by many sorting and ordered-container operations. Ask about self-comparison, contradictory directions, transitivity, and equivalence groups. A comparator using less-than-or-equal is not a valid substitute for strict precedence. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: F.4 External operations and evidence
keyPoints: Completion.
The point at which an operation’s required result has been checked, distinct from eventual destructor cleanup.
Ask whether final output, flush, or close failures are observed before success is reported.
Ordinary completion is not automatically crash durability.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 27, treat F.4 External operations and evidence as a design decision with costs and evidence. Completion. The point at which an operation’s required result has been checked, distinct from eventual destructor cleanup. Ask whether final output, flush, or close failures are observed before success is reported. Ordinary completion is not automatically crash durability. Deterministic fixture. A saved input and expected contract whose result can be compared directly. Ask whether the expectation is hand-derived or independent of the implementation under test. A seed alone may not reproduce a library distribution’s exact generated sequence across implementations. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.
